A separate panel in April allowed the Pentagon to maintain a policy requiring journalists to make appointments to interview officials and staff, which it added after the initial press policy was struck down.

WASHINGTON (CN) â The Justice Department on Monday urged a D.C. Circuit panel to maintain the Pentagonâs restrictive press policy, specifically a requirement that journalists be escorted at all times within the complex, suggesting the government has the right to fully close the Pentagon to reporters.

The three-judge panel heard consolidated Pentagon appeals challenging Senior U.S. District Judge Paul Friedmanâs summary judgment ruling that its press policy and subsequent escort requirement violated the First and Fifth Amendments.

On Oct. 6, 2025, the Pentagon announced a policy allowing journalists to be labeled a âsecurity riskâ for reporting classified or unclassified information without authorization. Dozens of major news outlets across the political spectrum refused to sign, leaving Trump-aligned journalists with âPentagon Facilities Alternate Credentials.â

The New York Times challenged the policy Dec. 4, 2025, arguing it discriminated against reporting disfavored by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. During litigation in spring 2026, the newspaper said the restrictions reversed longstanding press access during wars and crises, including Sept. 11, 2001, as the U.S. conducted strikes on Venezuela and entered a war with Iran.

Senior U.S. Circuit Judge Judith Rogers pressed the Justice Department on the limits of its position, citing the Supreme Courtâs view that reporters âroaming the hallsâ of government serve the public and âhelps aid the security of this nation and of our democracy.â

Justice Department attorney Sean Janda argued that the Pentagon is a nonpublic forum under the First Amendment, like an airport terminal or polling place, where the government may reasonably restrict speech and journalists have no inherent right of access.

âThey have no right in the first instance under the First Amendment to be in the Pentagon, which is closed to the public, and they have no right to get access to government information, which is not being provided to the public,â Janda said. âThe cases are exceedingly clear that the government can close a non-public forum to all expression if itâs doing so in an even-handed basis.â

U.S. Circuit Judge Patricia Millett emphasized that news gathering is central to journalism, questioning a provision that presumes reporters knowingly âferreted outâ unauthorized information unless they provide sufficient evidence otherwise.

The Barack Obama appointee said the standard, which resolves doubts in the Pentagonâs favor, exceeds criminal evidentiary standards.

Theodore Boutrous of Gibson Dunn, representing the New York Times, argued the presumption effectively puts âjournalism on trialâ whenever reporters use unauthorized information.

He urged the panel, which also included Senior U.S. Circuit Judge Karen Henderson, a George H.W. Bush appointee, to reinstate Friedmanâs summary judgment order lifting the escort requirement.

On April 27, a separate panel allowed the escort requirement to remain during the appeal, finding the Pentagon likely to succeed in arguing the provision was not properly before Friedman because it was absent from the original 2025 policy.

Three days after Friedman granted the Times summary judgment on March 20, the newspaper reported that the Pentagon had introduced an interim policy retaining many restrictions on journalists and adding the escort requirement.

#7496. 10th Circuit skeptical of expanding Oklahoma juvenile parole rights

A man convicted in a triple murder committed when he was 15 says Oklahoma unconstitutionally fails to take age during the crime into consideration during parole reviews.

(CN) â An attorney for Dwain Edward Thomas told a 10th Circuit panel Monday that the Eighth Amendment requires states to treat parole review for juvenile homicide offenders differently from adults.

âMr. Thomas was only 15 when he committed his crimes, a child both physically and mentally,â Caroline Robinson of Kirkland & Ellis said. âThe Oklahoma parole system fails this constitutional mandate.â

The three-judge panel must decide if Oklahoma must build youth consideration into every stage of parole review for juvenile homicide offenders, or whether the Eighth Amendment only requires discretion at sentencing. The amendment protects from excessive bail and fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

Robinson argued that Oklahoma never ensures decision makers know if they are dealing with a juvenile or that they weigh subsequent maturity and rehabilitation throughout the parole process.

U.S. Circuit Judge Jerome A. Holmes, a George W. Bush appointee, asked what prevented the Oklahoma parole board from considering age.

Robinson said the investigative reports do not reliably convey it, with only one report explicitly stating Thomasâ age at the time of the offense. She said board members reviewing 250 to 500 cases a month cannot be expected to calculate ages at the time of offense in every case.

âThe parole board members need to be given the means and the information in order to be able to apply the meaningful opportunity,â she said, adding that in some earlier reports age had been treated as an aggravating factor.

U.S. Circuit Judge Carolyn B. McHugh observed that the reports contain birth dates and case file years, and that in 2016 and 2019, investigators recommended parole in part because of Thomasâ youth.

Robinson said that constitutional protection must apply every time, not only when someone happens to notice and rely on it.

âWhat we are asking you to tell Oklahoma is that, in consideration of juvenile offenders, only juveniles are entitled to this Eighth Amendment protection and meaningful consideration must be afforded,â she said.

McHugh noted that U.S. Supreme Court precedent in Miller v. Alabama addressed mandatory life without parole sentences for juvenile homicide offenders and Graham v. Floridaâs âmeaningful opportunityâ standard applied to non-homicide cases.

The Barack Obama appointee also asked whether Robinson was seeking a rule the court has not adopted for someone sentenced to life with parole.

Robinson said the principles already support relief.

âGraham held that a state must give juvenile offenders a meaningful opportunity to obtain release based on demonstrated maturity and rehabilitation,â she said, adding that nothing in the cases makes the protections crime-specific.

William Patrick Flanagan, representing Oklahoma officials, argued that the Supreme Court has required only a discretionary sentencing process that considers youth before imposing life without parole.

âWhen Thomas was a juvenile offender, he was afforded precisely that process and he was awarded a life sentence with the possibility of parole,â Flanagan said, emphasizing that Thomasâ claim demands a mandatory, specific criterion at every stage of parole review â an extension no appeals circuit has accepted.

âExisting Supreme Court precedent does not require that the pardon and parole board and the entire apparatus that Oklahoma provides have a specific criterion that they are mandated to consider juvenile status at the time of the crime,â Flanagan argued.

Holmes asked whether Thomas was also arguing that Oklahomaâs system is a âfull-on shamâ that effectively converts life with parole into life without parole. Flanagan said no; the claim is limited to the absence of a required youth consideration.

McHugh asked whether a purely sham process would violate the Eighth Amendment. Flanagan agreed it would raise concerns, but said that is not the argument presented.

On rebuttal, Robinson clarified that the claim is that the system fails to provide a meaningful opportunity for juvenile offenders because it is not structured to consider juvenile status throughout.

âNot just mandated, but even if they wanted to, they donât have the tools or information necessary to be able to,â she said, distinguishing her case from a claim that no one can ever obtain parole.

The panel did not make any decision Monday and took the case under submission.

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Justice Pierce Butler, who served on the Supreme Court from 1923 to 1939, died on this day in 1939. Butler was the first Minnesotan appointed to the Supreme Court and the only dissenter in the infamous case of Buck v. Bell (though he did not write anything).

On Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, they announced that they had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, a dispute over whether a financial-services company violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering. For more on these cases, see the On Site section below.

Additional orders from Friday’s conference are expected this morning at 9:30 a.m. EST.

The December session of oral arguments will begin on Nov. 30.

#7493. Immigration agents’ seizure of lawyer’s phone at airport appears retaliatory, judge finds

A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at a Boston airport in 2025. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at the Boston Logan International Airport in September 2025.

U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the District of Massachusetts also found that federal agents likely violated the First Amendment rights of Andrew Lattarulo, a co-owner of the law firm Georges Cote in Massachusetts. Lattarulo runs an Instagram account featuring videos explaining immigrants’ rights and critiquing federal immigration policies.

After agents seized Lattarulo’s phone without a warrant and downloaded a copy of its contents, they returned the phone. The government has claimed that the seizure was part of an investigation into his firm for potentially employing unauthorized immigrants.

Lattarulo’s lawsuit alleges that agents targeted him because of his advocacy and seized information that included confidential communications with his clients.

Burroughs’ ruling mandates that federal officials preserve all copied cellphone data without accessing it as litigation continues, according to a story by Law.com.

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, a Bill Clinton appointee in the Southern District of New York who died last month, rebuffed those efforts.

On Monday, Trumpâs defense attorney Robert Giuffra from Sullivan & Cromwell argued he was entitled to removal to federal court because it was timely filed within 60 days of the Supreme Courtâs July 2024 ruling in Trump v. United States, which gave former presidents absolute immunity for duties within their core powers and some immunity for other official actions.

âThe appeal of this unprecedented criminal case brought by the state of New York against the president of the United States belongs in federal court,â Giuffra said. “This case involves important questions of presidential evidentiary immunity that arose out of the Supreme Court’s landmark decision in Trump v. United States.â

Superior Court, claiming fraud and abuse of process; it was dismissed sua sponte, and Harris appealed to the D.C. Court of Appeals. The Department of Transportation filed a notice of removal in federal district court and the Superior Court but did not notify the appeals court until more than a month later. In federal court, Harris amended his complaint, and DOT moved to dismiss, which the court granted.

Walker acknowledged Harris dealt with the issue but asked how that applies to a federal circuit appeals panel taking on such a case.

âI’m asking now about an appeal here and whether we would then just be asked to review the cases, as we would as if the trial court, state trial court, was a district court, and rule on the issues there,â the George H.W. Bush appointee said.

âI mean, this was obviously a local hush money case, but on the other hand, once you get into questions about evidence relating to what went on in the Oval Office or what the president may have done, then you have to look at the immunity point, notwithstanding the fact that it’s a local,â the judge said.

Trumpâs defense recently argued a separate appeal of the conviction before a state appeals court â New Yorkâs Appellate Division, First Department â where a panel of five judges mulled over Trumpâs defense team’s claims that presidential immunity and federal preemption should justify dismissal more than two years after the trial.

In a letter to the Second Circuit, Trumpâs lawyers said it would be âunfairâ for the federal appeals panel to consider that the First Department has heard oral argument as a reason to deny removal.

#7491. Container Engineer at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of new databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

Container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

We expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for new platform capabilities and major changes.

Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):

Tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers). You reason about trade-offs rather than reaching for defaults.

Software engineering — write real production code (Go and/or a comparable systems language) and can build controllers, operators, and platform APIs — stepping back to the underlying problem and building the right solution when no off-the-shelf tool fits.

Operational / SRE practice — are fluent in SLOs, error budgets, and operational KPIs; have led incident response and blameless postmortems; and have driven down MTTD/MTTR for systems you operated.

Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems and understand isolation as a spectrum — from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and resource quotas through to stronger primitives such as virtual clusters (e.g. vCluster) or VM-class runtimes.

Operate confidently on AWS (multiple accounts, IAM, VPC) and are comfortable with infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine) and Kubernetes.

Script and automate to eliminate toil rather than absorb it.

Communicate clearly with both infrastructure specialists and product engineers, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

Experience building and operating a multi-tenant Kubernetes platform that internal teams deploy onto.

Familiarity with policy engines (Kyverno, or OPA/Gatekeeper) and cost-attribution tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) for per-tenant chargeback/showback.

Experience with managed database platforms or Postgres.

Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

New remote jobs delivered to your inbox, every week.

Location independence is the future of work. It serves companies with best talent from around the globe. And benefits employees with a greater work life balance and the ability to work in their pyjamas.- Nithur, founder.
